prompt: Clinical contact surfaces should be

options.text: Barrier-protected and/or cleaned and disinfected between patients
Sterilized with a chemical sterilant at the start of each day
Wiped with a disinfectant only when blood is visible on them
Cleaned with soap and water between patients without disinfecting

explanation: Between-patient surface asepsis prevents cross-infection. Use an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant.

distractorExplanations.b: Sterilants and high-level disinfectants are not for environmental surfaces, and once-daily treatment misses between-patient turnover.
distractorExplanations.c: Clinical contact surfaces are contaminated by spatter and gloved hands even without visible blood; treat them every patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleaning removes soil but clinical contact surfaces also need an EPA-registered disinfectant when not barrier-protected.

prompt: After the last patient leaves, an assistant sprays the operatory floor and the painted walls with the same hospital disinfectant just used on the light handles. How should those floors and walls be managed?

options.text: Disinfect them between every patient, using the same product as on the light handles
Clean them on a schedule, and disinfect them when they are visibly soiled
Leave them for a weekly mop, because patients seldom touch the floor or walls
Apply a chemical sterilant each morning so the floors and walls stay sterile

explanation: Floors and walls are housekeeping surfaces. They are cleaned on a schedule and whenever they are soiled, including blood or other body fluids. They are not disinfected between every patient the way a clinical contact surface is.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a floor and a wall like a clinical contact surface. Housekeeping surfaces are not disinfected between every patient.
distractorExplanations.c: A weekly delay leaves soil in place. Housekeeping surfaces are cleaned on a schedule and whenever they are soiled.
distractorExplanations.d: Chemical sterilants are for heat-sensitive instruments, not for floors and walls in an operatory.

prompt: Barriers (plastic covers) on light handles should be

options.text: Changed at the end of each day unless they become visibly soiled
Wiped with disinfectant between patients and reused while intact
Changed between patients and surfaces cleaned if contamination occurred
Replaced between patients by staff still wearing contaminated gloves

explanation: Barriers are single-patient; clean underlying surfaces on contamination/scheduled basis per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Barriers are single-patient items; leaving one in place all day carries contamination from patient to patient.
distractorExplanations.b: Barrier film is meant to be discarded after each patient; wiping it does not reliably decontaminate and defeats its purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: Remove barriers with gloved hands, then remove gloves and perform hand hygiene before placing new barriers with clean hands.

prompt: Dental unit waterlines should deliver water that

options.text: Is sterile water for routine restorative care as well as for surgical irrigation
Meets potable standards once lines are flushed for 2 minutes each morning
Is safe once the unit's antiretraction valves are working properly
Meets drinking-water standards for routine care (≤500 CFU/mL heterotrophic bacteria)

explanation: DUWL maintenance and monitoring reduce biofilm risks; sterile water is required for certain surgical irrigations. That ≤500 CFU/mL figure is the common benchmark, maintained through monitoring and maintenance.

distractorExplanations.b: Flushing temporarily lowers counts but does not remove biofilm; waterline treatment and monitoring are still required.
distractorExplanations.c: Antiretraction valves prevent suck-back of oral fluids but do nothing to control biofilm in the waterlines.

prompt: The first patient is seated and the assistant reaches for the air-water syringe, but no one has run water through the lines since the previous afternoon. What does flushing those lines now, and again between patients, accomplish?

options.text: It lowers planktonic bacteria that built up inside the waterlines
It sterilizes the handpiece, so the handpiece can skip the sterilizer
It takes the place of biological monitoring for the office sterilizer
It removes any need to clean and disinfect clinical contact surfaces

explanation: Flushing at the start of the day and between patients, as the unit instructions direct, washes planktonic bacteria out of the lines. Flushing does not remove biofilm. Treatment and monitoring are still required so treatment water meets the CDC recommendation of ≤500 CFU/mL of heterotrophic water bacteria.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a waterline flush with sterilization of the handpiece. Handpieces are heat-sterilized after each patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses waterline flushing with sterilizer monitoring. Biological indicators are still used to check the sterilizer.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses waterline care with surface asepsis. Clinical contact surfaces still need a barrier or disinfection between patients.

prompt: Which waste is typically regulated as medical/biohazard waste in dentistry?

options.text: Any item that touched the patient's mouth, including lightly stained gauze
Sharps and items saturated with blood/saliva that drip when compressed
All gloves and masks used chairside, even if not saturated with blood
Extracted teeth containing amalgam, which go in the red biohazard bag

explanation: Regulated waste definitions are specific—sharps and saturated infectious items; follow local rules. Definitions vary, so follow local regulations.

distractorExplanations.a: Lightly soiled gauze is generally ordinary waste; regulated waste is sharps and items that release blood or saliva when compressed.
distractorExplanations.c: Used gloves and masks that are not saturated are usually general waste; red-bagging everything inflates cost without a rule basis.
distractorExplanations.d: Amalgam teeth must not go in red bags destined for incineration, which releases mercury; they are handled as amalgam waste.

prompt: Extracted teeth with amalgam should be

options.text: Placed in the red biohazard bag for medical-waste incineration
Heat-sterilized before being returned to the patient or donated to a dental school
Handled as potential biohazard and amalgam-containing waste per EPA/state rules
Placed in the sharps container with used needles and blades

explanation: Amalgam/mercury disposal has special environmental rules; treated teeth may be returned under policies. They must not be incinerated as ordinary trash, which vaporizes mercury.

distractorExplanations.a: Medical-waste incineration vaporizes the mercury in amalgam, so amalgam-containing teeth stay out of red-bag incineration.
distractorExplanations.b: CDC advises against heat-sterilizing amalgam teeth because heat releases mercury vapor; formalin immersion is used for school use.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharps containers are usually incinerated or autoclaved, both of which can release mercury from amalgam restorations.

options.text: PPE, then disinfectant sprayed on the blood and wiped off immediately

PPE, absorbent removal of bulk soil, then EPA-registered disinfectant

Sterilization reduces pathogens to safe levels; disinfection destroys all microbial life on items
Disinfection destroys spores given enough contact time; sterilization just shortens the process

distractorExplanations.b: High-level disinfection kills most microbes but not high numbers of bacterial spores at standard contact times; only sterilization does.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the definitions: disinfection reduces pathogens, while sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores.

Removing barriers, cleaning/disinfecting clinical contact surfaces
Spraying surfaces with disinfectant and placing barriers before wiping
Wiping surfaces with a dry towel, then covering them with fresh barriers

explanation: Systematic between-patient IPC protects the next patient. Sharps and waste are also managed safely during turnover.

Sprayed with disinfectant and covered with a barrier without precleaning

prompt: During a filling, the assistant's gloves touch the overhead light handle and the chair control switches. Before the next patient is seated, what should be done with those handles and switches?

options.text: Wipe them at closing time if no blood is visible on the plastic
Leave the morning barrier in place when the film still looks intact
Wash them with detergent and skip a disinfectant because they are metal
Apply a fresh barrier, or clean and disinfect them, before the next patient

explanation: Light handles and chair switches are clinical contact surfaces. Between patients they receive a new barrier, or they are cleaned and disinfected with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant. A barrier left from the previous patient carries that contamination forward.

distractorExplanations.a: Visible blood is not the deciding point. Gloved hands and spatter contaminate these controls during each appointment.
distractorExplanations.b: A surface barrier is single-patient. Leaving it on moves the last patient's contamination to the next person in the chair.
distractorExplanations.c: Detergent removes some soil but does not replace disinfection when these clinical contact surfaces are left uncovered.

prompt: Dental unit waterlines should be maintained so water quality

options.text: Meets dental water standards (eg, ≤500 CFU/mL heterotrophic bacteria for non-surgical use)
Is sterile for every procedure because tap water cannot be used in dental units
Is acceptable once lines are flushed for 20–30 seconds at the start of each clinic day
Is checked by the unit's in-line filter, which removes the need for water testing

explanation: Waterline biofilms need active management and monitoring. Flushing and waterline treatment protocols maintain that level.

distractorExplanations.b: Sterile water is required only for surgical procedures; nonsurgical care uses water meeting the ≤500 CFU/mL standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Flushing helps but does not eliminate biofilm; CDC still expects waterline treatment and periodic monitoring.
distractorExplanations.d: In-line filters reduce bacteria but can fail or be colonized; monitoring is still needed to confirm water quality.

Placed in a sealed red bag lined with a second plastic bag
Collected in an empty plastic bottle, then sealed in the regular trash

prompt: After a blood spill on a counter, you should

options.text: Disinfect with a low-level product first, then clean up the remaining blood afterward
Wipe with a damp towel, then apply a sterilant such as glutaraldehyde
Contain, clean, and disinfect with an appropriate intermediate-level disinfectant
Cover with a barrier film and disinfect at the end of the clinic day

prompt: Blood from a scaling appointment has spotted the bracket-table handle. The assistant reaches for a glass cleaner stored in the staff kitchen. Which product belongs on that handle?

options.text: An EPA-registered intermediate-level hospital disinfectant labeled for blood
The kitchen glass cleaner, since the spot is small and the handle looks smooth
A chemical sterilant such as glutaraldehyde poured onto the bracket table
Plain soap and water with no disinfectant, as if the table were a floor

explanation: A bracket-table handle is a clinical contact surface, and blood is present. Remove the soil, then use an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant with an intermediate-level claim for blood. Household glass cleaner is not that product, and chemical sterilants are not for environmental surfaces.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a household glass cleaner with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant. Blood on a clinical contact surface needs the hospital product.
distractorExplanations.c: Glutaraldehyde and other chemical sterilants are for heat-sensitive instruments, not for wiping a bracket-table handle.
distractorExplanations.d: Soap and water can preclean, but blood on a clinical contact surface also needs an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant.

prompt: While changing the cover on the air-water syringe holder, the assistant notices the cover was torn and the holder underneath is wet from spray. What should happen before a new cover is placed?

options.text: Clean and disinfect the holder, then place the new cover with clean hands
Lay the new cover over the wet holder so the tear stays hidden from view
Wipe the holder with a dry paper towel and put the new cover on right away
Leave the torn cover in place until the end of the day, then replace it

explanation: A torn barrier can let spray reach the surface under it. That holder is cleaned and disinfected before the next barrier goes on, and the new cover is placed with clean hands. Covering a wet surface, or waiting until the end of the day, passes contamination to the next patient.

distractorExplanations.b: Hides the contamination instead of removing it. A new barrier over a wet, soiled holder traps debris against the surface.
distractorExplanations.c: A dry towel does not disinfect. Spray on the holder has to be cleaned away and the surface disinfected before it is covered.
distractorExplanations.d: A torn barrier is not left for later patients. The exposed surface is cleaned and disinfected, then a new barrier is placed.

prompt: Halfway through a procedure the assistant needs more cotton rolls and reaches into the large jar with the same gloves that have been in the patient's mouth. What is the safer retrieval?

options.text: Dispense with sterile cotton pliers, or use rolls set out before gloving
Reach in with the treatment gloves, then wipe the jar rim with alcohol
Dump the leftover rolls into the sink, rinse them, and return them to the jar
Tip the jar onto the bracket table with those gloves, then put unused rolls back

explanation: Bulk cotton is retrieved aseptically so saliva on the treatment gloves does not seed the jar for later patients. Sterile pliers, or rolls set out before the gloves go on, keep the supply clean. Wiping the rim does not decontaminate rolls the gloves already touched.

distractorExplanations.b: Contaminated gloves transfer saliva into the bulk supply. Wiping the rim afterward does not make the touched cotton safe for later patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Rinsing cotton in the sink does not restore a contaminated bulk jar, and wet rolls put back in the jar stay contaminated.
distractorExplanations.d: Tipping the jar with saliva-coated gloves contaminates the rolls that spill, and putting unused rolls back seeds the supply.

prompt: A disposable saliva ejector was used on one patient. It looks clean after a rinse, so the assistant hangs it on the unit for the next person. What should happen to that ejector?

options.text: Soak it in a surface disinfectant and reuse it for the rest of the morning
Discard it after this patient and open a new ejector for the next person
Run it through the ultrasonic cleaner and store it with the sterile packs
Wipe it with alcohol and save it in case this patient returns next week

explanation: A disposable saliva ejector is a single-use device. Rinsing, soaking, or wiping it does not make it safe for another use, including a later visit by the same patient. It is discarded, and the next patient receives a new ejector.

distractorExplanations.a: A surface disinfectant does not reprocess a single-use saliva ejector. The device is discarded after one use.
distractorExplanations.c: Ultrasonic cleaning is for reusable instruments. A disposable ejector is not processed and stored with sterile packs.
distractorExplanations.d: Single-use means one procedure, not one patient saved for a later visit. Alcohol does not make the ejector reusable.

prompt: A fluoride-varnish jar is shared by several patients. The assistant is about to put a brush that just touched the teeth back into that jar. What is the correct practice?

options.text: Put the brush back in, then wipe the jar threads before the lid goes on
Use a single dose dispensed before treatment, and do not reenter the jar
Put the brush back in, then add disinfectant so the varnish stays usable
Put the brush back in and write today's date on the lid for the next patient

explanation: Varnish used for more than one patient is dispensed as a single dose so a used brush does not go back into the container. Reentering the jar contaminates the remaining varnish. Disinfectant in the jar does not restore a contaminated supply.

distractorExplanations.a: Wiping the threads does not fix varnish that a used brush has entered. The container should not be reentered during treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: Disinfectant added to the jar contaminates the material and does not make a reentered multi-use container safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Dating the lid does not control contamination. A used brush left in the jar seeds the varnish for the next patient.

prompt: A surgical extraction needs irrigation. The unit water met the CDC limit of ≤500 CFU/mL on the last test for routine dental treatment water. The dentist plans to irrigate through the standard unit syringe. Which delivery is appropriate?

options.text: The standard unit syringe, because a passing check means the water is sterile
Sterile saline or sterile water in a sterile syringe, separate from the unit line
Sink tap water poured into the unit bottle and sent through the unit line
The unit syringe after an extra flush, using the same nonsterile delivery path

explanation: Routine dental treatment water is held to ≤500 CFU/mL of heterotrophic water bacteria, which is not sterile. Surgical irrigation uses sterile water or sterile saline delivered through a sterile device. The standard unit waterline and an extra flush do not provide that sterile delivery.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the routine dental-unit water standard with sterility. Meeting ≤500 CFU/mL does not make unit water sterile enough for surgery.
distractorExplanations.c: Tap water run through the unit line is still unit water. Surgery needs sterile irrigant and a sterile delivery path.
distractorExplanations.d: An extra flush does not sterilize the line or the water. Surgical irrigation needs sterile fluid and sterile delivery.

prompt: The high-volume evacuator trap is full of debris at the end of the day. An assistant lifts the trap insert out over the sink with bare hands. How should that trap be cleaned?

options.text: Keep using bare hands, then wash with soap once the trap insert is empty
Empty the insert while wearing utility gloves, a mask, and eye protection
Leave the debris until the weekly service visit so staff do not open the trap
Rinse the insert with the patient's mouth rinse and snap it back on the hose

explanation: Evacuator traps hold blood, saliva, and debris. Staff clean them on a schedule while wearing utility gloves, a mask, and eye protection, not with bare hands. Leaving a packed trap in service, or rinsing it with mouth rinse, does not make the task safe.

distractorExplanations.a: Bare hands on a trap expose skin to blood and debris. Utility gloves, a mask, and eye protection are worn for this task.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for an outside service visit leaves a full trap in use. Staff clean traps on schedule while wearing the right protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Mouth rinse is not a cleaner for a contaminated trap, and snapping a dirty insert back on returns debris to the line.

prompt: During a full-mouth series the gloved assistant touches the digital sensor and the tube-head handles. Before the next patient, how are that sensor and those handles managed?

options.text: Heat-sterilize both with the instrument packs because they were in the room
Wipe both at closing, treating radiography equipment as a housekeeping surface
Cover and disinfect the sensor; barrier or disinfect the tube-head handles
Place covers in the morning and leave those same covers on for the whole day

explanation: A digital sensor is semicritical because it contacts oral mucosa. At a minimum, cover it with an FDA-cleared barrier and, after that barrier is removed, clean and disinfect it with an intermediate-level hospital disinfectant the manufacturer allows. Heat-sterilize or high-level disinfect the sensor only when its instructions allow that. Tube-head handles are clinical contact surfaces: a new barrier, or cleaning and disinfection, between patients.

distractorExplanations.a: The tube head does not go in the instrument sterilizer. Heat-sterilize a sensor only when its manufacturer allows that cycle; most do not. Being in the room is not the reason to sterilize either one.
distractorExplanations.b: A tube-head handle is a clinical contact surface, and a sensor is semicritical. Neither is a housekeeping surface left until closing.
distractorExplanations.d: A cover left on all day carries the last patient's contamination forward. Change the sensor barrier between patients, then disinfect the sensor after the barrier comes off.

prompt: An alginate impression is rinsed and sealed in a damp bag while still coated with saliva and blood, ready for the laboratory driver. What should happen before it leaves the office?

options.text: Send the bag as packed and let the laboratory disinfect it when they can
Heat-sterilize the impression so the laboratory receives a sterile cast
Rinse, use a compatible intermediate-level hospital disinfectant, rinse, and send
Hold it in a chemical sterilant until the driver arrives, then ship it wet

explanation: Impressions leave the mouth coated with saliva and blood. They are rinsed, disinfected with an EPA-registered intermediate-level hospital disinfectant that is compatible with the material, then rinsed again before the laboratory receives them. A still-contaminated bag is not the handoff.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaves a contaminated impression in the bag. The dental office disinfects the impression before the laboratory receives it.
distractorExplanations.b: Heat will distort alginate and is not how impressions are prepared. Disinfection, not sterilization, is the laboratory handoff.
distractorExplanations.d: A chemical sterilant is the wrong product for an impression and can damage the material. Use a compatible hospital disinfectant.

prompt: A partial denture returns from the laboratory in a closed bag. The assistant is ready to seat it in the patient's mouth directly from that bag. What comes first?

options.text: Seat it right away, because the laboratory already sterilized every case
Rinse it under tap water and seat it while the appliance is still wet
Disinfect it with a compatible hospital disinfectant, rinse it, then seat it
Keep it dry in the bag and seat it at the next visit with no further care

explanation: Appliances returning from the laboratory are disinfected before they go into the patient's mouth. Use an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant compatible with the prosthesis, then rinse so residual chemical is not seated against tissue. A tap-water rinse does not disinfect it.

distractorExplanations.a: Assumes the laboratory sterilized the case. The dental office disinfects the prosthesis before it is seated in the mouth.
distractorExplanations.b: A tap-water rinse removes loose debris but does not disinfect the prosthesis before it contacts oral tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting until the next visit does not disinfect the appliance. It is disinfected and rinsed before it is placed.

prompt: After an extraction, one gauze square drips blood when squeezed, and the patient napkin beside it shows a few light saliva marks. How are the two items discarded?

options.text: Both items go in the red biohazard container because each one also touched the patient
Both items go in ordinary trash because gauze and napkins are not sharps
The dripping gauze is regulated waste; the lightly marked napkin is ordinary trash
The napkin goes in the sharps container and the dripping gauze goes in the trash

explanation: Regulated medical waste includes items so saturated with blood or saliva that they drip when compressed. A lightly marked napkin is ordinary office trash. Touching the patient does not by itself make an item regulated waste, and a napkin is not a sharp.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats every patient-contact item as regulated waste. Light saliva on a napkin does not meet the saturated, dripping standard.
distractorExplanations.b: Ignores saturation. Gauze that drips blood when squeezed is regulated waste even though it is not a sharp.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps the containers. The dripping gauze is the regulated item, and a napkin does not belong with sharps.

prompt: The curing-light handle is coated with composite dust and saliva. The assistant sprays disinfectant and immediately presses a new barrier onto the still-crusted handle. What sequence is required?

options.text: Leave the new barrier over the crust so the spray can work underneath it
Skip the cleaning, because the new barrier makes disinfectant unnecessary
Scrape the crust off with a fingernail and cover the handle with no disinfectant
Preclean, apply an intermediate-level disinfectant, then cover the handle

explanation: Saliva on the handle is other potentially infectious material, and the composite crust blocks a disinfectant. Preclean that soil, then apply an EPA-registered intermediate-level hospital disinfectant with a tuberculocidal claim. Cover the handle only after that. A low-level product is not enough when saliva is visible, and a barrier pressed onto the crust seals the contamination in place.

distractorExplanations.a: Traps soil under the barrier. Disinfectant cannot work through composite crust, so the handle is cleaned before it is covered.
distractorExplanations.b: A barrier does not replace cleaning and disinfection of a handle that is already soiled. The soil has to come off first.
distractorExplanations.c: A fingernail is not a cleaning method, and skipping disinfectant leaves a clinical contact surface untreated between patients.

prompt: Suction hoses ran through a full afternoon of surgery and are being left overnight with debris still inside. In the morning a quick water rinse is suggested. How should these lines be maintained?

options.text: A morning water rinse is enough, because the hose stays outside the mouth
Run the chemical sterilant used on heat-sensitive burs through the hose
Cap the hoses and wait until the trap is changed sometime next month
Clean them with an evacuation cleaner on the schedule in the unit instructions

explanation: Evacuation lines collect blood and debris and are cleaned with a cleaner made for the suction system, on the schedule in the unit instructions. A water rinse does not replace that cleaner, and an instrument sterilant is not an evacuation-line product.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a water rinse as full line maintenance. Debris in suction hoses needs an evacuation-system cleaner, not water alone.
distractorExplanations.b: Instrument sterilant is the wrong product for suction lines and can damage the system. Use the evacuation cleaner the unit instructions name.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting until next month's trap change leaves contaminated lines in service. Lines are cleaned on the unit's own schedule.

prompt: After an exposure, the assistant peels open a saliva-covered phosphor-plate packet with freshly washed hands, touching the outside, then sets the plate on the counter. How should that packet be opened?

options.text: Grasp the saliva-covered outside with the washed hands, then lift the plate
Spray the outside of the packet, then lift the plate with those same hands
Lay the plate on the counter and wipe it with alcohol after handling the outside
Open it so clean hands meet the plate and avoid the saliva-covered outside

explanation: The outside of an intraoral phosphor-plate packet is contaminated with saliva. Clean hands touch the plate, not that outside. Touching the outside and then the plate, or the counter, carries oral microorganisms onto the image receptor and the work surface.

distractorExplanations.a: Handwashing does not decontaminate a saliva-covered packet. Clean hands that then touch the outside become contaminated again.
distractorExplanations.b: Spraying the outside does not replace an aseptic opening. Hands that touched the packet still transfer saliva to the plate.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiping the plate afterward does not undo transfer that already happened. The opening has to keep saliva off the plate.

prompt: After a routine exam the assistant drops dry examination gloves, a mask, and a cotton roll with a faint saliva tint into the red biohazard container. Where should those items go?

options.text: Leave them in the red container; anything that touched the mouth is regulated waste
Shift the cotton roll to the sharps container and keep the gloves and mask in red
Place the gloves, mask, and cotton roll in the sharps container with the needles
Put them in ordinary trash; they are not saturated with blood and are not sharps

explanation: Gloves, masks, and lightly stained cotton are ordinary waste when they are not so saturated that blood or saliva drips out. The red container is for regulated waste, and the sharps container is for sharps. Autoclaving those items does not change how they are sorted.

distractorExplanations.a: Overclassifies patient-contact items. A faint saliva tint does not make gloves, a mask, or a cotton roll regulated waste.
distractorExplanations.b: A cotton roll is not a sharp, and unsaturated gloves and masks do not belong in the biohazard container.
distractorExplanations.c: A sharps container is for devices that can puncture skin. Unsaturated gloves, a mask, and a cotton roll are ordinary trash, not sharps.

prompt: The correct general sequence for reusable instruments is

options.text: Transport, clean, package, sterilize, store
Sterilize first, then clean heavily soiled instruments
Store dirty, then sterilize without cleaning
Package before removing bioburden

explanation: Cleaning must precede sterilization; soil interferes with sterilization.

distractorExplanations.b: Sterilizing dirty instruments fails.

prompt: After an extraction, a coworker takes a bloody forceps out of the ultrasonic tank and sets it in the clean drawer, saying the cycle finished the instrument. The tank run should be understood as

options.text: Completed disinfection, so the forceps can go back in the drawer with no autoclave cycle
Soil removal by cavitation, with rinsing, packaging, and sterilization still required
A substitute for the steam sterilizer when the next patient needs that forceps quickly
Proof the forceps are sterile, because the solution was warm and the timer finished

explanation: Cavitation loosens blood and debris from instrument surfaces. That is cleaning, not sterilization. A critical forceps is still contaminated when it leaves the tank and still has to be rinsed, inspected, packaged, and heat-sterilized.

distractorExplanations.a: The tank does not disinfect. Cavitation removes soil, and the forceps are not ready for the clean drawer.
distractorExplanations.c: An ultrasonic unit cannot stand in for a sterilizer. A critical forceps still needs a sterilization cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: A warm bath and a finished timer do not show sterility. The unit cleans debris and leaves the forceps unsterile.

prompt: Instrument cassettes help primarily by:

options.text: Allowing instruments to skip cleaning because cassettes shield them from debris
Serving as the sterilization wrap so no pouch or wrap is needed in the autoclave
Keeping sets together and reducing sharps handling injuries during processing
Reducing the need for chemical indicators inside each wrapped set

explanation: Cassettes improve safety/organization but cleaning/sterilization still required.

distractorExplanations.a: Cassettes hold instruments during processing, but the instruments inside still go through ultrasonic or washer cleaning.
distractorExplanations.b: Most cassettes are perforated and must still be wrapped or pouched to maintain sterility after the cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Each wrapped cassette still needs an internal chemical indicator; cassettes organize sets but do not replace process monitoring.

prompt: Chemical indicators on packages show

options.text: That the sterilizer killed spores, so weekly biological monitoring can be skipped
That the load is sterile once the external tape changes color, without other checks
That the instruments were cleaned of bioburden before packaging
That sterilizing conditions were present, not that every item is sterile

explanation: External/internal chemical indicators are process monitors showing sterilizing conditions were present—not necessarily that every item is sterile; biologic indicators verify sterilizer kill. Each indicator responds to the specific parameters (e.g., temperature/steam exposure) it is designed for.

distractorExplanations.a: Spore kill is verified only by biological indicators; chemical indicators do not replace weekly spore testing.
distractorExplanations.b: External tape only shows the package went through a cycle; it does not prove sterility of the contents.
distractorExplanations.c: Chemical indicators respond to sterilizer conditions, not to cleaning quality; residual debris is checked by inspection.

prompt: Biological indicators (spore tests) should be used

options.text: At least weekly to verify sterilizer lethality
Once a month, with chemical indicators covering the weeks between tests
Only after sterilizer repairs, with chemical indicators used day to day
Quarterly, as required for steam sterilizers under OSHA rules

explanation: CDC recommends routine BI monitoring; implant loads need BI results before use when required. CDC also calls for a biological indicator with every load containing an implantable device.

distractorExplanations.b: Monthly testing is below the CDC weekly minimum, and chemical indicators cannot substitute for spore testing.
distractorExplanations.c: Spore testing after repairs is required in addition to, not instead of, routine weekly biological monitoring.
distractorExplanations.d: CDC (not OSHA) sets the at-least-weekly biological monitoring guidance; quarterly testing is far too infrequent.

prompt: A positive spore test (failed BI) should lead to:

options.text: Rerun the spore test and keep using the sterilizer while awaiting the result
Take the sterilizer out of service and do not use loads until failures are resolved
Recall only loads containing implants and keep processing other instruments
Switch to a chemical vapor cycle on the same unit without investigating the failure

explanation: Failed BI indicates possible sterilization failure—quarantine and investigate. Recall and reprocess affected loads per policy.

distractorExplanations.a: CDC calls for removing the sterilizer from service while the failure is retested and investigated, not continued use.
distractorExplanations.c: A positive BI means every load since the last negative test may be unsterile; recall is not limited to implant loads.
distractorExplanations.d: The failure must be investigated (loading, cycle parameters, equipment) before the unit is used again in any cycle.

prompt: Flash/immediate-use steam sterilization should be

Used for implant trays, which can then be stored wrapped for later use
Used only for emergencies when no sterile replacement exists
Used in place of precleaning when an instrument is needed quickly

explanation: IUSS is for urgent situations with strict controls—not routine processing. It is not a routine convenience or a substitute for adequate inventory.

prompt: When loading a sterilizer, packages should be:

options.text: Packed tightly and stacked flat to maximize each cycle's load
Laid flat with pouches stacked plastic side down in layers
Loaded with cassettes touching the chamber walls to use all space
Arranged to allow steam/air circulation—not overloaded or stacked

explanation: Steam must contact all surfaces; follow manufacturer loading instructions. Follow the sterilizer and packaging IFU so steam can penetrate every package.

distractorExplanations.a: Overloading and flat stacking block steam penetration and drying, a common cause of sterilization failure and wet packs.
distractorExplanations.b: Pouches should stand on edge or be spaced so steam reaches the paper side; stacked layers trap air and moisture.

prompt: A hemostat is placed in a peel pouch with the ratchet clicked shut so the beaks stay together. Before the pouch is sealed for the autoclave, the assistant should

options.text: Release the ratchet and leave the hinge fully open and unlocked for the cycle
Keep the first ratchet click so the beaks cannot shift inside the pouch
Lock the hinge now and open it after the cycle so the joint can dry
Close the hinge for the autoclave after leaving it open in the ultrasonic tank

explanation: Steam has to reach the box lock and the mating surfaces of a hinge. A ratchet left clicked, even at the first notch, holds those surfaces together. Hinged instruments are packaged and sterilized open and unlocked so the sterilant contacts the joint.

distractorExplanations.b: A clicked ratchet keeps the joint closed, so steam cannot reach the box-lock surfaces. Keeping the beaks aligned is not a reason to lock it.
distractorExplanations.c: Opening the joint after the cycle is too late. Surfaces that stayed closed were not exposed to steam.
distractorExplanations.d: The hinge stays open for cleaning and for sterilization. Closing it before the autoclave blocks the joint during the cycle.

prompt: Which statement about event-related shelf life is correct?

options.text: Sterility lasts exactly 24 hours regardless of packaging
Sterile packages remain usable until an event compromises integrity (tear, moisture, expiration if dated), if storage is proper
Packages may be stored under sinks in puddles
Open packages can be resealed with tape for sterile use

explanation: Event-related sterility depends on package integrity and storage conditions.

distractorExplanations.a: Time-related policies vary; not universally 24h.
distractorExplanations.c: Wet storage contaminates.
distractorExplanations.d: Opened packages are not sterile.

prompt: A scaler still carries dried blood. An assistant is about to seal it in a pouch and autoclave it, then scrub tomorrow if any debris remains. The processing order should

options.text: Autoclave the scaler first, then wash off whatever soil is left on it
Skip the scrub when the film looks light, and go straight to the pouch
Remove the dried blood first, then package and sterilize the scaler
Seal the bloody scaler now and rely on steam to bake the debris off

explanation: Bioburden shields microorganisms from the sterilant. Blood and debris are removed, the scaler is rinsed and inspected, and then it is packaged and sterilized. A cycle run on a soiled instrument is not a reliable sterilization process.

distractorExplanations.a: Sterilizing before washing leaves soil in place, and that soil blocks steam from contacting the metal.
distractorExplanations.b: A light film of blood is still bioburden. Looking nearly clean is not a reason to skip the cleaning step.
distractorExplanations.d: Steam does not reliably penetrate dried blood. Debris is cleaned off before the scaler is packaged.

prompt: An assistant fills the ultrasonic tank, sets a cassette in the basket, and starts the cycle with the cover left on the counter so the instruments stay in view. The correct setup is

options.text: Leave the cover off so staff can see that cavitation is moving the instruments
Start uncovered, then set the cover in place if the solution begins to splash
Leave the cover resting ajar so a long cycle does not overheat the tank
Seat the cover fully, then start the cycle so the spray stays inside the tank

explanation: The cover stays on while an ultrasonic cleaner runs. Cavitation throws contaminated solution into the air, and an open tank spreads that spray through the processing area. The lid is closed before the cycle starts and stays closed until the cycle stops.

distractorExplanations.a: Watching the instruments does not justify an open tank. An open cycle releases contaminated spray into the room.
distractorExplanations.b: The cover belongs on for the whole cycle. Putting it on after splashing starts still releases aerosol first.
distractorExplanations.c: A gap vents contaminated aerosol into the room. Fear of overheating is not a reason to leave the cover unseated.

prompt: Chemical indicators on packs primarily show

options.text: That sterilizer process conditions for that indicator type were met
That instruments are sterile and ready for implant procedures
That spores were killed, replacing weekly biological monitoring
That instruments were cleaned and free of bioburden before packaging

explanation: Indicators monitor process conditions; biologic monitoring verifies sterilizer performance on a schedule. A chemical indicator alone does not prove the items are sterile.

distractorExplanations.b: Implant loads need a negative biological indicator before release; a chemical indicator does not prove sterility.
distractorExplanations.c: Only biological indicators test spore kill; chemical indicators supplement but never replace weekly spore testing.
distractorExplanations.d: Indicators react to sterilizer conditions such as temperature and steam, not to how well instruments were cleaned.

options.text: Sterilized closed on the first ratchet to keep tips aligned
Sterilized in the open/unlocked position
Sterilized closed, then opened after the cycle to dry the joints
Wrapped closed inside a cassette that holds them in position

prompt: A wet pack after a steam cycle should be

options.text: Dried on the counter, then stored as sterile if the indicator changed
Used first, the same day, before contamination can wick through
Considered compromised for sterility assurance and reprocessed
Accepted if the internal chemical indicator shows a full color change

explanation: Wet packs can wick contaminants; reprocess. Reprocess per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Moisture lets microbes wick through the wrap; drying afterward does not restore sterility, even with a passed indicator.
distractorExplanations.b: A wet pack is treated as contaminated immediately; using it quickly does not make it sterile.
distractorExplanations.d: The indicator shows the cycle conditions were met but says nothing about contamination wicking through a wet wrap.

prompt: Contaminated burs and a scaler are carried from the operatory toward the processing room in an open hand. The transport step should use

options.text: A closed, leak-proof, puncture-resistant container taken to decontamination
An open tray held at waist height so coworkers can see the sharps and step aside
A paper-towel wrap carried past sterile storage to save a second trip
The same gloved hand, rinsed at the operatory sink, then walked into packaging

explanation: Contaminated instruments move in a covered, puncture-resistant, leak-proof container straight to the decontamination area. An open hand or an open tray can drop sharps and can drip blood along the route, including through clean zones.

distractorExplanations.b: An open tray still lets instruments fall and lets blood drip. Transport uses a closed, rigid container.
distractorExplanations.c: Paper does not contain leaks or punctures, and the route should not pass through sterile storage.
distractorExplanations.d: Rinsing a glove does not make loose contaminated instruments safe to carry into the packaging area.

prompt: To shorten the walk, sterile pouches are kept on an open shelf directly above the ultrasonic tank. That storage choice

options.text: Breaks one-way flow, because finished packs do not belong in decontamination
Saves time, because the autoclave door is nearby and the pouches stay in reach
Is acceptable when the shelf is wiped with the same detergent used in the tank
Works if each pouch faces plastic-side out so spray cannot mark the paper

explanation: Instrument processing moves one way, from dirty to clean: decontamination, then packaging, then sterilization, then sterile storage. Keeping finished packs above the ultrasonic tank puts sterile items back in the contaminated zone, where spray can wet them.

distractorExplanations.b: A shorter walk does not remove the contamination risk. Finished packs are stored outside the decontamination room.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiping the shelf with tank detergent does not turn a dirty room into sterile storage. The packs need a clean, dry cabinet.
distractorExplanations.d: Pouch direction does not protect packs from ultrasonic spray. The shelf itself is in the wrong zone.

prompt: Blood and cement have dried on a curette. An assistant picks up dish soap and a green scouring pad. Cleaning should rely on

options.text: An instrument detergent, then a water rinse, following that curette's IFU
The scouring pad alone, because rubbing matters more than which soap is used
Dish soap left to dry on the metal so the film can protect it until the autoclave
A splash of ultrasonic solution wiped on the tip, with the residue left in place

explanation: Dental instruments are cleaned with a detergent suited to them, often an enzymatic cleaner when blood and protein have dried, then rinsed so residue does not stay on the metal. The curette IFU governs the cleaner. Household soap and abrasive pads can leave film or scratch the surface.

distractorExplanations.b: Scrubbing dried cement with an abrasive pad can scratch the curette. The cleaner and the method have to match the IFU.
distractorExplanations.c: Dried dish soap is residue, not protection. Residue can interfere with sterilization and can irritate tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: A wipe of cleaning solution is not a completed cleaning step, and leftover detergent has to be rinsed off.

prompt: A surgical bur entered bone during an extraction. The bur is heat-stable, and it will be used on another patient. Spaulding processing calls for

options.text: Heat sterilization between patients, because the bur is a critical item
High-level disinfection, treating bone contact as a semicritical exposure
A surface disinfectant wipe, because the bur is small and the schedule is tight
Ultrasonic cleaning alone, because cavitation reaches between the flutes

explanation: Under Spaulding, an item that enters bone, soft tissue, or the vascular system is critical. A heat-stable critical item is heat-sterilized between patients. Cleaning comes first, and a wipe or an ultrasonic cycle does not replace the sterilizer.

distractorExplanations.b: Bone entry is critical, not semicritical. High-level disinfection is the path for heat-sensitive semicritical items.
distractorExplanations.c: A wipe does not sterilize a critical bur. A tight schedule does not change the Spaulding category.
distractorExplanations.d: The ultrasonic cleaner removes debris from the flutes. It does not sterilize a critical instrument.

prompt: A reusable impression tray contacts oral mucosa. The manufacturer states that steam will warp it, and no heat cycle is allowed. The processing step is

options.text: Heat sterilization anyway, because every item placed in the mouth is critical
High-level disinfection, the Spaulding path for a heat-sensitive semicritical item
Soap and water, because a tray that cannot be autoclaved cannot be made safe
A rinse and a closed drawer, because mucosa contact counts as noncritical

explanation: A device that contacts mucous membrane but does not enter sterile tissue is semicritical. When that device cannot tolerate heat, Spaulding calls for high-level disinfection. A steam cycle would damage this tray, and a soap rinse does not reach high-level disinfection.

distractorExplanations.a: Mucosa contact without entry into sterile tissue is semicritical, not critical, and this tray's IFU forbids heat.
distractorExplanations.c: Inability to tolerate steam does not end processing. Heat-sensitive semicritical items still receive high-level disinfection.
distractorExplanations.d: Mucous-membrane contact is semicritical, not noncritical. A rinse and a drawer do not disinfect the tray.

prompt: A heat-stable mouth mirror contacted oral mucosa and did not enter soft tissue or bone. Before another patient, the mirror should receive

options.text: Low-level disinfection, because a mirror does not break the mucosa
Heat sterilization, the preferred step for a heat-stable semicritical item
High-level disinfection, because heat is reserved for items that enter bone
A water rinse, because the mirror is metal and saliva is not blood

explanation: Mouth mirrors contact mucous membrane, so they are semicritical. Heat-stable semicritical items are heat-sterilized rather than held at disinfection. This mirror tolerates heat, so after cleaning the sterilizer is the right method.

distractorExplanations.a: Low-level disinfection fits some noncritical surfaces. A mirror contacts mucosa and, when heat-stable, is heat-sterilized.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat sterilization is not limited to bone-entry items. Heat-stable semicritical instruments are heat-sterilized too.
distractorExplanations.d: Saliva on a mucosa-contacting mirror is not handled by a rinse alone. The mirror is cleaned and then heat-sterilized.

prompt: A peel pouch for a forceps has no internal strip, and the date is written in ballpoint ink across the paper panel. Before the pouch is loaded, the assistant should

options.text: Leave the ink on the paper, because that is the panel steam still has to pass through
Add an internal indicator and move the date and load notes onto the plastic panel
Skip the internal strip, because external tape will be stuck on at the autoclave
Seal the pouch as marked, then write the missing load number after the cycle

explanation: Ink on the paper side of a peel pouch can damage the barrier steam must pass through, so the date and load notes go on the plastic. Each package also gets a chemical indicator. Tape added outside later does not fix a pouch sealed with no internal indicator.

distractorExplanations.a: Writing on the paper can damage the barrier. Labels go on the plastic panel, not across the paper.
distractorExplanations.c: External tape does not replace an indicator inside the package. The strip goes in before the pouch is sealed.
distractorExplanations.d: Load identity is written before sterilization. Adding it afterward leaves the pack unlabeled for the cycle and for storage.

prompt: The steam sterilizer has finished exposure, and the drying phase has not started. The next patient needs a pouch from that load. The assistant should

options.text: Remove that pouch now and fan it until the paper feels dry to the touch
Let the drying phase finish, then let the packs cool before unloading
Cancel drying so the chamber can be reloaded for the next cassette
Unload the pouches while hot and set them in a drawer to finish drying

explanation: Packs taken out before the drying phase finishes come out wet. Moisture can wick contamination through the wrap, and handling hot, damp packs adds more moisture. Drying is allowed to finish, and the packs cool before they are touched or stored.

distractorExplanations.a: Fanning a pouch outside the chamber does not replace the drying phase, and a damp barrier is already a problem.
distractorExplanations.c: Canceling drying to free the chamber produces wet packs. Drying is part of the cycle, not spare time.
distractorExplanations.d: A hot stack in a drawer traps moisture against the pouches. They stay in the cycle until they are dry.

prompt: Sterile pouches are kept in a drawer under the operatory sink, beside a damp trap. The better storage place is

options.text: That same drawer, with a towel under the pouches to catch drips from the trap
The counter above the utility sink, so the packs stay close to the operatory
A clean, dry, closed cabinet kept away from sinks, splash, and wet floors
The cabinet under the decontamination sink, if each pouch still looks sealed

explanation: Sterile packs stay sterile while the barrier stays intact and dry. A drawer under a sink exposes them to leaks and splash, and moisture wicking through a pouch ends sterility. Store them in a clean, dry, closed cabinet, separate from sinks and from decontamination.

distractorExplanations.a: A towel does not stop splash from reaching the pouches, and a damp towel itself wets the barriers.
distractorExplanations.b: A counter beside a sink is still a splash zone. Finished packs need a closed, dry cabinet.
distractorExplanations.d: A sealed look does not protect packs stored in a wet cabinet. Storage has to be clean and dry.

prompt: A surgery pouch shows darkened external tape and was sealed with no strip inside. The dentist asks to open it for a critical forceps. The assistant should

options.text: Open it, because a color change on the tape is enough to release a critical forceps
Open it for this patient, then place a strip in the next pouch from this unit
Do not release it, because external tape alone does not prove the contents were sterilized
Accept the tape as this week's spore test and record the load as biologically monitored

explanation: A chemical indicator shows that the condition it is built to detect, such as heat or steam contact, was met. An indicator on or in every package is still not proof of sterilization by itself. External tape with no internal strip does not establish that the forceps are sterile.

distractorExplanations.a: External tape can change without proving the inside of the pouch was sterilized. It is not a release test for a critical forceps.
distractorExplanations.b: Fixing the next pouch does not rescue this one. This package has no internal indicator and should not be treated as verified.
distractorExplanations.d: Tape is a chemical indicator, not a spore test. It cannot be logged as biological monitoring of the sterilizer.

prompt: Midway through a steam cycle the sterilizer alarms. The printout shows the chamber did not reach temperature, and the door has been opened. Instruments from that load should be

options.text: Released, because the external tape had already started to darken before the alarm
Dried on the counter and stored, because the door was open for a short time
Treated as unsterile and reprocessed in a full cycle after the unit is checked
Set aside as immediate-use items and stored in a cabinet for the next day

explanation: A cycle that did not reach temperature did not sterilize the load, and opening the door ends it. The instruments are not released. The sterilizer is checked for the malfunction, and the instruments are reprocessed in a completed cycle.

distractorExplanations.a: A partial color change does not rescue a cycle that did not reach temperature. The load is not released.
distractorExplanations.b: Air-drying on the counter does not finish a failed cycle. The instruments were not sterilized.
distractorExplanations.d: Immediate-use steam is not a storage method, and an aborted cycle did not sterilize these instruments for later use.

prompt: The sterilizer manual lists a common gravity-displacement cycle of 121°C (250°F) for 30 minutes and a common prevacuum cycle of 132°C (270°F) for 4 minutes. A wrapped cassette IFU requires the prevacuum cycle. The assistant should

options.text: Run the gravity cycle, because a longer exposure must be the stronger steam cycle
Pick whichever saved cycle finished fastest on the previous instrument load
Use the gravity cycle for this wrapped cassette and save prevacuum for handpieces
Select the prevacuum cycle named by the cassette IFU and the sterilizer manual

explanation: Cycle choice follows the instrument IFU and the sterilizer manual. A common gravity-displacement cycle is 121°C (250°F) for 30 minutes, and a common prevacuum cycle is 132°C (270°F) for 4 minutes. This cassette calls for the prevacuum cycle, so that is the cycle selected.

distractorExplanations.a: A longer gravity exposure is not automatically the right cycle. This cassette IFU requires prevacuum, and the manual authorizes the settings.
distractorExplanations.b: Speed from a previous load is not how a cycle is chosen. The IFU and the sterilizer manual set the cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: A wrapped cassette is not automatically a gravity load. This IFU specifies prevacuum, so gravity would be the wrong cycle.

prompt: The extraoral shield on a curing light contacts intact skin and is classified as noncritical. Between patients, routine processing of that shield is

options.text: Heat sterilization, because every item used beside a patient is treated as critical
High-level disinfection, because skin contact places it with semicritical devices
A pass through the ultrasonic tank, because noncritical devices are cleaned there
Cleaning and disinfection of the surface, without sterilization as the routine

explanation: Spaulding reserves sterilization for critical items and for heat-stable semicritical items. A device that contacts intact skin is noncritical. The routine is cleaning and disinfection of that surface, not a sterilizer cycle and not an ultrasonic bath meant for soiled instruments.

distractorExplanations.a: Use beside the patient is not the same as entering tissue. Intact-skin contact is noncritical and is not routinely sterilized.
distractorExplanations.b: Semicritical items contact mucous membrane or nonintact skin. Intact skin is the noncritical category.
distractorExplanations.c: The ultrasonic tank is for cleaning soiled instruments, not the routine step for a noncritical intact-skin surface.

prompt: In the cabinet, a forceps pouch has a split along the seal, and the indicator strip is visible through the gap. Before the forceps are used, the assistant should

options.text: Tape the split shut and return the pouch to the cabinet for a later patient
Use the forceps today, because the strip inside had already changed color
Wipe the beaks with disinfectant and skip a full cleaning and sterilization cycle
Reprocess the forceps, because a broken seal means the pack is no longer sterile

explanation: Sterility of a stored pack depends on an intact, dry barrier. A split seal is an event that compromises the pouch, so the forceps are not used from it. They go back through cleaning, packaging, and sterilization.

distractorExplanations.a: Tape does not restore a sterile barrier. A torn pouch is reprocessed, not patched and returned to the cabinet.
distractorExplanations.b: A changed strip shows cycle conditions were met at the time. It does not keep the forceps sterile after the seal splits.
distractorExplanations.c: A disinfectant wipe does not replace reprocessing. The forceps are cleaned, repackaged, and sterilized.

prompt: After a completed steam cycle, one pouch's internal strip is still the starting color, while the external tape on that same pouch has changed. The forceps in that pouch should be

options.text: Released, because the external tape changed and that result overrides the internal strip
Released and logged as a passed spore test, since one mark on the pouch responded
Stored at the front of the cabinet so they are used while the cycle is recent
Reprocessed, because an unchanged internal indicator means the package is not released

explanation: An internal chemical indicator that does not change means that package is not released, even when external tape on the same pouch changed. The failed internal result controls. The forceps are reprocessed. A chemical indicator is still not a biological spore test.

distractorExplanations.a: External tape does not overrule a failed internal indicator. The package is not released when the internal strip does not change.
distractorExplanations.b: A chemical indicator is not a spore test. Logging it as biological monitoring misstates both the failed strip and the monitor type.
distractorExplanations.c: Putting the pouch at the front of storage treats it as sterile. An unchanged internal strip means the pack is not released.

prompt: OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard requires employers to:

options.text: Establish an exposure control plan, offer HBV vaccination, provide PPE, and train employees
Establish an exposure control plan and require HBV vaccination as a condition of hire
Provide PPE and annual training, with HBV vaccination costs paid by the employee
Train employees every three years and review the exposure control plan as needed

explanation: BBP Standard mandates plans, engineering/work controls, PPE, vaccine offer, and training.

distractorExplanations.b: OSHA requires HBV vaccine to be offered free, and employees may decline by signing a declination; it cannot be a hiring condition.
distractorExplanations.c: The employer must offer HBV vaccination at no cost to employees with occupational exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: BBP training is required at assignment and annually, and the exposure control plan must be reviewed at least annually.

prompt: After a needlestick from a used instrument, the employee should

options.text: Squeeze the site to bleed it, apply bleach, and report at the end of the day
Wash the site, report immediately, and follow post-exposure evaluation
Wash the site, then report only if the patient's history shows HIV or hepatitis
Wash the site and start PEP within 7 days if the source tests positive

Hazard labels for secondary containers, replacing the written HazCom program
Hazard information and safe handling/PPE guidance for chemicals

prompt: Which is a work-practice control?

options.text: Recapping only with a one-handed scoop technique
Installing sharps containers at the point of use in each operatory
Using a safety syringe with a self-sheathing needle
Wearing puncture-resistant utility gloves during instrument cleanup

explanation: Work-practice controls change how tasks are performed to reduce exposure. Two-handed recapping is not acceptable; a safer mechanical method may also be used.

distractorExplanations.b: A sharps container is an engineering control that isolates the hazard, not a change in how the task is performed.
distractorExplanations.c: Safer sharps devices are engineering controls built into equipment; work-practice controls change worker behavior.
distractorExplanations.d: Utility gloves are personal protective equipment, a separate category from work-practice controls.

Available, accessible, and flushed/maintained per requirements
Located within a one-minute walk and flushed once each month
Installed at a sink and tested once a year during the OSHA review

explanation: Prompt irrigation capability is required for chemical exposures. This applies where corrosive chemicals are used.

distractorExplanations.c: ANSI Z358.1 calls for reaching the station in about 10 seconds and activating plumbed units weekly.

prompt: During nitrous oxide sedation, the assistant hears gas hissing because the nasal hood sits loosely on the patient's face. What should be corrected?

options.text: Switch the scavenging vacuum off until the patient says the hood feels comfortable.
Raise the nitrous flow so sedation holds even though the hood is leaking gas.
Reseat the nasal hood until it seals, and keep the scavenger on for the procedure.
Place a HEPA room purifier by the chair and leave the loose hood where it is.

explanation: A nasal hood has to seal, and the scavenger has to stay on, so exhaled nitrous is captured at the patient. A loose hood leaks gas into the operatory even when the unit is running.

distractorExplanations.a: Turning the scavenger off for comfort dumps exhaled nitrous into the room instead of capturing it at the hood.
distractorExplanations.b: More flow through a hood that does not seal increases the leak; the fix is a fitted hood, not a higher setting.
distractorExplanations.d: A HEPA purifier captures particles and does not remove nitrous oxide gas, so it cannot replace a seal or a scavenger.

prompt: Which training topic is required under OSHA BBP for dental employees with exposure risk?

options.text: Hazard communication labeling, SDS use, and chemical spill cleanup
Fire extinguisher use, evacuation routes, and emergency action plans
Radiation safety, film handling, and dosimeter badge procedures
Modes of transmission, PPE use, and exposure response

explanation: BBP training covers exposure prevention and response; employers document training. Training also covers engineering and work-practice controls, and it must be documented.

distractorExplanations.a: Those are Hazard Communication Standard topics; BBP training covers bloodborne transmission, PPE, and exposure response.
distractorExplanations.b: Those fall under OSHA's emergency action and fire prevention rules, not the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Radiation safety is governed by state radiation rules, not the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens training requirement.

prompt: A courier is due for biohazard pickup, and blood-soaked gauze still sits in an open bin with a clear liner. What container standard must be met first?

options.text: Use a closable, leak-resistant container that is color-coded or biohazard-labeled.
Keep the clear liner, as long as the gauze is tied off before the courier arrives.
Pack the bin past the fill line so fewer containers leave with the courier.
Leave a household trash liner in place if the outside of the bin has a sticker.

explanation: Regulated medical waste must go in a closable container that holds the contents without leaking and is red or labeled with the biohazard symbol so haulers can identify it.

distractorExplanations.b: A clear liner hides regulated waste from handlers; the bag itself has to be red or carry the biohazard label.
distractorExplanations.c: Filling past the line causes spills and punctures during pickup; the container is closed and replaced before it is overfull.
distractorExplanations.d: A sticker on the outer bin is not enough once the liner is removed; the liner has to stay identified as regulated waste.

prompt: Which statement about tuberculosis infection control in dentistry is correct?

options.text: Patients with latent TB infection should be treated in airborne isolation rooms
Patients with infectious TB should have elective care deferred
Patients with active TB can be treated routinely if staff wear surgical masks
Elective care can proceed once a patient with active TB has started medication

explanation: Airborne TB requires special handling beyond Standard Precautions alone. Urgent care uses airborne precautions or referral as appropriate.

distractorExplanations.a: Latent TB infection is not contagious; airborne precautions are for suspected or confirmed active TB disease.
distractorExplanations.c: Surgical masks do not filter TB droplet nuclei; active TB calls for deferral or treatment with N95 respirators and airborne precautions.
distractorExplanations.d: Starting treatment is not enough; elective care waits until a physician confirms the patient is no longer infectious.

prompt: The OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard requires employers to:

options.text: Establish an exposure control plan and require HBV titers before hiring
Offer HBV vaccination within 30 days of hire and review the plan every five years
Establish an exposure control plan and offer HBV vaccination to at-risk employees
Keep exposure records only for the length of each employee's employment

explanation: Exposure control plans and HBV offers are core OSHA BBP elements.

distractorExplanations.a: OSHA requires offering HBV vaccination after assignment, not pre-hire titers; post-vaccination titer testing is a CDC follow-up.
distractorExplanations.b: The vaccine is offered within 10 working days of assignment, and the exposure control plan is reviewed at least annually.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA requires exposure and medical records to be kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years.

prompt: After a needlestick, the injured worker should generally

Wash the site and get tested in 6 months before filing a report
Wash the site, report promptly, and follow post-exposure evaluation protocol
