prompt: The manager is revising the exposure-control plan and wants a control that isolates contaminated needles before hands touch them. Which choice belongs on that list?

options.text: A puncture-resistant sharps container at chairside and a needle that sheaths itself.
A posted rule to recap with one hand and to wash hands before leaving the room.
Exam gloves, a surgical mask, and eyewear worn while the injection is given.
A staff lecture on stick injuries plus a sign-in sheet filed with the roster.

explanation: Sharps containers and self-sheathing needles are engineering controls because they isolate the needle. Recapping rules and handwashing change behavior, gloves are protective equipment, and a lecture is training.

distractorExplanations.b: One-handed recapping and handwashing are work-practice controls; they change how the task is done and do not isolate the needle.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves, masks, and eyewear are personal protective equipment, worn after engineering controls, not a device that isolates the sharp.
distractorExplanations.d: A lecture and a roster are training records; they do not physically separate staff from a contaminated needle.

prompt: The ultrasonic-solution Safety Data Sheet is already in the binder, but a new employee cannot explain the label warnings. What should happen before she uses that chemical?

options.text: Let her mix the solution today and put label training on a later staff-meeting agenda.
Train her on the label, the Safety Data Sheet, PPE, and first aid before she starts.
Show the bloodborne-pathogens slides and count that class as her chemical-safety training.
Give her the staff nickname for the solution and skip the printed hazard warnings.

explanation: Hazard Communication training has to cover labels, the Safety Data Sheet, protective equipment, and first aid before she works with the chemical. A binder on the shelf does not replace that training.

distractorExplanations.a: Putting training on a later agenda leaves her handling a hazardous chemical before Hazard Communication instruction.
distractorExplanations.c: Bloodborne-pathogens class covers blood exposure, not chemical labels, Safety Data Sheets, or chemical first aid.
distractorExplanations.d: A nickname hides the product and its hazards; training uses the real label and the Safety Data Sheet, not a shop name.

prompt: Minutes after putting on powdered latex exam gloves, an assistant develops hives and itchy hands. What should the office supply for her clinical work?

options.text: A second pair of latex gloves worn over the first pair during patient care.
Powder-free latex gloves used in place of non-latex exam and utility gloves.
A latex-free kit with non-latex exam gloves and non-latex utility gloves.
Cotton liners under the same latex gloves as the main hand protection.

explanation: A latex-sensitive employee needs latex removed from her tasks, including a latex-free kit for exams and instrument cleanup. Another latex layer, powder-free latex, or a cotton liner still leaves latex protein on the skin.

distractorExplanations.a: Doubling latex gloves increases contact with latex protein; it is not a substitute for a latex-free kit.
distractorExplanations.b: Powder-free latex still contains latex proteins; dropping the powder does not make the glove safe for an allergic employee.
distractorExplanations.d: Cotton liners may ease irritation, but they do not block latex protein, so they are not the protection she needs.

prompt: A newly hired hygienist will scale teeth and handle blood-soaked gauze, but the written exposure-control plan does not list those tasks. What should the manager do?

options.text: Revise the plan so the new tasks, controls, and job title are listed before she starts.
Leave the plan unchanged until an injury shows that an update is actually needed.
Take the written plan down and rely on the workplace poster in the break room.
Drop her job description into the chemical-safety binder and call that the update.

explanation: The exposure-control plan has to match the tasks people actually perform. New scaling and blood-handling duties, the controls for them, and the job title go into the plan before she starts that work.

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for an injury leaves an exposure task uncovered; the plan is updated when duties change, not after someone is hurt.
distractorExplanations.c: A workplace poster does not list task-specific controls or job titles, so it cannot stand in for the written plan.
distractorExplanations.d: A job description in the chemical binder is not the exposure-control plan and does not document bloodborne controls.

prompt: A new assistant begins chairside cleanup this morning and will contact blood during that work. When is the hepatitis B vaccine offered, and who pays?

options.text: Within 10 working days of this assignment, at no cost to the employee.
Within 10 working days of this assignment, with the fee taken from her pay.
After her first needlestick, at no cost if she is still on the payroll.
After she sends a written request, with the clinic setting the fee.

explanation: Under the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, hepatitis B vaccination is offered at no cost within 10 working days of initial assignment to tasks with exposure. The employee does not pay the fee, and the offer is not delayed until an injury.

distractorExplanations.b: The 10-working-day timing is right, but the employer pays; deducting the fee from her paycheck violates the no-cost offer.
distractorExplanations.c: The offer is tied to assignment to exposure tasks, not to a later needlestick, even though the vaccine would still be free.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for a written request and charging a clinic fee misses both the 10-working-day deadline and the no-cost requirement.

prompt: An inspector asks how long the office must keep bloodborne-pathogens training sign-in sheets. What retention applies to those training records?

options.text: Keep each sign-in sheet for 3 years from the date of that training session.
Keep each sign-in sheet for the length of employment plus 30 years, like a medical file.
Keep each sign-in sheet through the first workweek, then shred the roster.
Keep each sign-in sheet for 30 years, including a sheet for someone who left the next day.

explanation: Bloodborne-pathogens training records are kept for 3 years from the training date. The employment-plus-30-years clock applies to employee medical records, not to sign-in sheets.

distractorExplanations.b: Employment plus 30 years is the medical-record rule; applying it to training sign-in sheets confuses the two retention clocks.
distractorExplanations.c: Shredding the roster after the first workweek destroys the training record long before the 3-year retention ends.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty years is the add-on for medical records after employment, not the retention period for a training sign-in sheet.

prompt: An employee resigns and leaves her hepatitis B vaccination record and a post-exposure medical file. How long are those medical records kept?

options.text: For 3 years, using the same clock as a bloodborne-pathogens training roster.
For the duration of employment plus 30 years after employment ends.
Until her resignation date, after which the medical file may be discarded.
Until the next safety walk-through, after which the medical file may be discarded.

explanation: Employee medical records, including hepatitis B vaccination status and post-exposure files, are kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years. Training rosters follow a different, shorter clock.

distractorExplanations.a: Three years is the training-record retention; vaccination status and post-exposure care are medical records, not sign-in sheets.
distractorExplanations.c: Discarding the file on the resignation date drops the required 30 years after employment ends.
distractorExplanations.d: A walk-through is not a retention date; medical records stay for employment plus 30 years regardless of the next inspection.

prompt: A scaler tip goes through an assistant's glove and into the skin while she is cleaning instruments. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Squeeze the site until it bleeds, then mention it at the next staff huddle.
Wash the site, report the injury immediately, and get a medical evaluation.
Wash the site, and file a report later if the chart lists a bloodborne disease.
Cover the site with a bandage and watch for symptoms before telling anyone.

explanation: After a puncture, wash the site, report immediately, and get a medical evaluation. That sequence starts follow-up while the details of the exposure are still fresh, whatever the chart appears to say.

distractorExplanations.a: Squeezing the wound to force bleeding is not recommended, and waiting for a huddle delays the report and the medical evaluation.
distractorExplanations.c: Every puncture is reported and evaluated; skipping the report unless the chart names a disease leaves unknown source status unchecked.
distractorExplanations.d: Watching for symptoms before telling anyone skips the immediate report and the medical evaluation the exposure requires.

prompt: The dentist asks the assistant to recap a used needle with both hands so it will not roll off the tray. What is the safer action?

options.text: Recap with both hands, because a small-gauge needle is unlikely to stick deeply.
Use a one-handed scoop or a recapping device, then discard it in the sharps container.
Bend the contaminated needle against the tray, then recap it with both hands.
Pass the uncapped needle to a coworker and ask that person to replace the cap.

explanation: If a contaminated needle must be recapped, use a one-handed scoop or a mechanical device, then put it in a sharps container. Two-handed recapping, bending the needle, and handing it off all move the point toward someone's hand.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping is the hazard the dentist just requested; needle gauge does not make that technique acceptable.
distractorExplanations.c: Bending a contaminated needle and then recapping with both hands adds two prohibited handling steps.
distractorExplanations.d: Handing an uncapped needle to a coworker moves the point toward another person instead of using a one-handed method.

prompt: Coffee cups sit on the bracket table between patients, in an area where blood spatter lands. What should the team change?

options.text: Add another sharps container and leave the cups on the bracket table.
Call a posted sign an engineering control and keep the drinks in the operatory.
Keep food, drinks, and cosmetics out of areas where blood exposure can occur.
Allow the drinks if each person wears exam gloves while holding the cup.

explanation: Eating, drinking, and handling cosmetics are prohibited where occupational exposure to blood can occur. That ban is a work-practice control: it changes behavior in the operatory rather than isolating the hazard with a device.

distractorExplanations.a: A second sharps container does not make drinks safe on a surface that gets blood spatter; the cups still have to leave the area.
distractorExplanations.b: A sign does not become an engineering control, and it does not authorize drinks where blood exposure is reasonably likely.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves on the hand that holds a cup do not lift the ban on food and drink in an exposure area.

prompt: A surface disinfectant is opened for the afternoon patients, and its Safety Data Sheet is missing from the office binder. What should happen before staff use it?

options.text: Borrow the sheet from a similar brand and assume the hazards and first aid match.
Skip the sheet because the bottle colors and the cap already warn the staff.
Obtain that product's Safety Data Sheet and keep it where staff can read it on shift.
Lock the copy at the owner's home so patients do not see the chemical name.

explanation: Each hazardous chemical needs its own Safety Data Sheet, readily available to employees during the work shift. Staff should have that sheet in hand before the product becomes part of routine use.

distractorExplanations.a: A similar brand can have different ingredients and first-aid steps; substituting its sheet leaves this product's hazards undocumented.
distractorExplanations.b: Bottle colors are not a Safety Data Sheet; Hazard Communication still requires the sheet for that specific product.
distractorExplanations.d: A sheet locked off site is not accessible during the shift, so employees cannot use it when they handle the chemical.

prompt: An assistant fills an unmarked spray bottle with instrument disinfectant for coworkers to use through the afternoon. What must that bottle display?

options.text: A staff nickname such as blue juice, with no hazard wording beside it.
No wording at all, because bottles filled for the same shift are exempt.
The product name and the hazard warnings from the original label or the SDS.
The name of the next patient, because the bottle will sit near an operatory.

explanation: A secondary container that other employees will use needs the product identity and the hazard warnings, taken from the original label or the Safety Data Sheet. A nickname does not carry those warnings.

distractorExplanations.a: A nickname such as blue juice replaces the product name and drops the hazard warnings coworkers need on a secondary bottle.
distractorExplanations.b: The immediate-use exception applies only to the employee who poured the chemical, and only during that same shift. It does not cover coworkers who will use the bottle through the afternoon.
distractorExplanations.d: The patient's name does not identify the chemical or its hazards, so it is not a Hazard Communication label.

prompt: Instrument disinfectant splashes into an assistant's eye at the processing sink. Using that product's first-aid directions, what should she do?

options.text: Wipe the eye with an alcohol pad from the same product line to counteract the chemical.
Finish the instrument load and read the first-aid section if her vision stays blurred.
Cover the eye and return to the sink so the instrument schedule stays on time.
Flush the eye with water and get medical care the sheet directs, with no neutralizer.

explanation: The Safety Data Sheet first-aid section for an eye splash calls for immediate flushing and medical care as directed. Putting another chemical in the eye to neutralize the splash can add injury.

distractorExplanations.a: Wiping the eye with an alcohol pad tries to neutralize or dry the splash and can worsen the injury instead of flushing it.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting until the load is done, and reading the sheet only if vision blurs, delays the flush the first-aid section calls for.
distractorExplanations.c: Returning to the sink to protect the schedule leaves the chemical in the eye and skips the flush and medical care.

prompt: A sales representative says one federal agency both writes dental infection-control guidelines and registers surface disinfectants. Which split of roles is accurate?

options.text: EPA publishes dental infection-control guidelines, CDC registers surface disinfectants, and FDA writes the exposure-control plan.
FDA publishes dental infection-control guidelines and also registers the surface disinfectants used on clinical contact surfaces.
CDC registers surface disinfectants, EPA clears heat sterilizers as medical devices, and FDA offers the hepatitis B vaccine.
CDC publishes dental infection-control guidelines, EPA registers surface disinfectants, and FDA clears heat sterilizers.

explanation: At the level dental teams use, CDC publishes infection-control guidelines, EPA registers surface disinfectants, and FDA clears medical devices such as heat sterilizers. One agency does not hold all three jobs.

distractorExplanations.a: This swaps CDC and EPA and assigns the exposure-control plan to FDA; that plan is the employer's OSHA document, not an FDA clearance.
distractorExplanations.b: FDA does not write the dental infection-control guidelines or register environmental surface disinfectants; those roles sit with CDC and EPA.
distractorExplanations.c: This swaps the device role and the disinfectant role, and hepatitis B vaccination is an employer duty under OSHA, not an FDA offer.

prompt: Packs from this morning were released for use even though the chemical indicators were not checked. How should this breach be handled?

options.text: Remove that day's sterilization pages so the gap is not visible later.
Keep seating patients with those packs and fix the paperwork at the next retreat.
Describe the breach aloud in the waiting room and skip an internal written note.
Stop using those packs, document the breach, and have the dentist judge patient risk.

explanation: Releasing packs without checking the chemical indicators is an infection-control breach. Stop using those instruments, write down what happened, and follow office policy so the dentist can evaluate patient risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling pages out of the log hides the breach instead of documenting it, and it leaves the suspect instruments in circulation.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuing to seat patients with those packs extends the breach. Fixing the paperwork later does not pull the instruments back.
distractorExplanations.c: A waiting-room announcement is not the evaluation step, and skipping the written note leaves the breach without a record.

prompt: The autoclave biological indicator from this morning shows growth, and packs from that load are still on the shelf. What should be written down and done next?

options.text: Replace the failed reading with a passing mark so the sterilization log shows no gaps at all.
Release the packs for use because the external indicator stripe changed color.
Jot the failure on a scrap of paper and throw that note away after lunch.
Record the failure, quarantine the load, and reprocess after the sterilizer is checked.

explanation: A biological indicator that shows growth means that load is not released. Record the failure in the sterilization log, quarantine the packs, and reprocess them after the sterilizer has been checked.

distractorExplanations.a: Changing a failed reading to a pass falsifies the sterilization log and hides a load that may not be sterile.
distractorExplanations.b: A color change on a chemical indicator does not override growth on a biological indicator; the load stays quarantined.
distractorExplanations.c: A scrap note that is discarded never becomes a sterilization record, so the failed cycle is lost.

prompt: A temporary assistant is scheduled for chairside assisting tomorrow and has not had bloodborne-pathogens training at this office. What must the employer do?

options.text: Let her assist and arrange training if a sharps injury happens on the job.
Hand her the chemical Safety Data Sheet binder and count that as bloodborne-pathogens training.
Ask her to sign a roster from an earlier session without attending the class.
Train her on transmission, controls, and post-exposure steps before she does tasks with exposure.

explanation: Employees with occupational exposure receive bloodborne-pathogens training before they perform those tasks. The session covers how bloodborne pathogens spread, the controls used in the office, and what to do after an exposure.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting until a sharps injury happens puts her in exposure tasks with no training on transmission, controls, or reporting.
distractorExplanations.b: The Safety Data Sheet binder is Hazard Communication material; it does not satisfy bloodborne-pathogens training.
distractorExplanations.c: Signing an old roster without the class creates a false training record and leaves her untrained for chairside exposure.

prompt: The operatory sharps container is filled past the marked line, and a needle hub protrudes from the opening. What should the assistant do?

options.text: Shake the container so the needles settle, then keep adding sharps past the line.
Reach in with a gloved hand and rearrange the needles until more space appears.
Empty the sharps into a tied trash bag and return that container to service.
Close it, set out a new puncture-resistant container, and do not push the contents down.

explanation: A sharps container that is past the fill line, or that has a sharp sticking out, is taken out of service. Close it, replace it with a puncture-resistant container, and do not push the contents down by hand.

distractorExplanations.a: Shaking an overfilled container and adding more sharps raises the chance of a stick; the container is replaced at the fill line.
distractorExplanations.b: Reaching in to rearrange needles puts a hand on contaminated sharps, which the container is meant to prevent.
distractorExplanations.c: Dumping sharps into a trash bag removes the puncture-resistant barrier and sends regulated sharps into ordinary trash.

prompt: Standard Precautions in dentistry mean staff should

options.text: Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
Apply PPE and extra precautions for patients with a known bloodborne infection
Treat blood as infectious but handle saliva as noninfectious unless visibly bloody
Change gloves between patients but skip hand hygiene when gloves were worn

explanation: Standard Precautions assume unknown infectious status; gloves do not replace hand hygiene. This includes using appropriate PPE and hand hygiene with every patient.

distractorExplanations.b: Precautions keyed to disclosed infection status are outdated; Standard Precautions apply to every patient because status is often unknown.
distractorExplanations.c: In dentistry saliva is treated as potentially infectious material; the bloody-saliva exception belongs to old Universal Precautions outside dentistry.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves can have micro-defects and hands get contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene is still required after gloves come off.

prompt: When is an N95 respirator typically indicated in dental settings (concept)?

options.text: For every brief hallway conversation with healthy staff
For procedures/situations with airborne risk per CDC/facility policy (e.g., certain airborne diseases), after fit testing
Instead of eye protection during splash procedures
Only as a fashion accessory

explanation: Respirators are for airborne hazards; splash protection still needs eyewear; fit testing matters.

distractorExplanations.a: Routine talk does not require N95.
distractorExplanations.c: Eye protection is separate for splashes.
distractorExplanations.d: Respirators are PPE, not fashion.

prompt: Hand hygiene should be performed

options.text: After removing gloves at the end of each patient, but not before gloving
Only when hands are visibly soiled, since glove use covers routine contact
Before donning gloves, after removing gloves, and whenever hands are contaminated
At the start and end of each shift, with glove changes covering patient contacts

distractorExplanations.b: Visible soil is the trigger for soap and water, not the only trigger; gloves never replace hand hygiene before and after patient care.
distractorExplanations.d: Shift-based hand hygiene ignores the per-patient moments around gloving; a glove change without hand hygiene leaves hands contaminated.

prompt: Which PPE combination is most appropriate for a procedure likely to produce splash of blood/saliva?

options.text: Gloves and a surgical mask, with eye protection reserved for the operator
Gloves and protective eyewear; a mask only when the patient reports a cough
Gloves, gown, and a face shield used in place of a mask and eyewear
Gloves, mask, and eye protection; gown when soiling of clothing is likely

explanation: Mucous membrane and clothing protection match splash risk. Eye protection may be goggles or a face shield.

distractorExplanations.a: The assistant sits in the same spatter zone as the operator, so eye protection is required for everyone exposed, not just the operator.
distractorExplanations.b: The mask protects the nose and mouth from blood/saliva splash on every spatter-generating procedure, not only for respiratory symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: A face shield can replace eyewear, but CDC still calls for a mask under it because spatter travels around the shield to the nose and mouth.

prompt: Utility gloves in instrument processing are worn to:

options.text: Protect hands during cleaning of contaminated instruments and handling chemicals
Serve as the sterile glove for minor surgical procedures after an autoclave cycle
Replace exam gloves for chairside patient care when a patient has a latex allergy
Be discarded after each use like exam gloves rather than washed and reused

distractorExplanations.b: Utility gloves are heavy puncture-resistant gloves for decontamination; surgical procedures require sterile surgical gloves.
distractorExplanations.c: Utility gloves are too bulky and are not patient-care gloves; a latex-allergic patient gets nitrile or other non-latex exam gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: Unlike exam gloves, utility gloves may be cleaned, disinfected, and reused until they crack, tear, or show other signs of deterioration.

prompt: Masks should be changed when:

options.text: At the end of each half-day session if they still look intact
They become wet, soiled, or between patients per protocol
Once daily, after the last patient, unless visibly torn
When they become wet, but the same mask may be kept on for several patients

distractorExplanations.c: Daily changes ignore moisture buildup and cross-patient contamination; masks are changed per patient and when wet or soiled.

prompt: A patient reports hives and lip swelling after a visit that used latex gloves. Before this appointment, the assistant should

options.text: Switch the patient to powder-free latex gloves, which remove the allergy risk
Treat the report as chapped skin and add lotion under a latex pair
Set up non-latex gloves and keep powdered latex out of this treatment room
Chart the allergy and let each clinician keep a usual glove brand

explanation: Hives and swelling after latex contact are an allergy to latex proteins, not dry-skin irritation. Powder-free latex still contains those proteins, and powder carries them through the air. This visit needs non-latex gloves, such as nitrile, with powdered latex kept out of the room.

distractorExplanations.a: Powder-free latex cuts down airborne powder but still contains latex proteins, so it leaves the allergen on a patient who already had hives and swelling.
distractorExplanations.b: Hives and swelling are an immune reaction to latex proteins, not irritant dermatitis. Lotion under latex gloves does not remove the allergen.
distractorExplanations.d: A chart note that still allows latex gloves leaves the allergen against the patient. Everyone working this appointment needs non-latex gloves.

prompt: The assistant finishes a prophy, drops the used gloves in the trash, and sees dry-looking hands. The immediate next step is to

options.text: Rub the eyelids to clear fogging before greeting the next patient
Dip the unwashed fingers into the shared lotion jar on the counter
Don the next pair right away while those hands still look dry
Clean the hands before touching the face, the chart, or clean items

explanation: The outside of the gloves holds saliva and blood, and peeling them off transfers that soil to the skin. Hand hygiene after removal is what keeps it off the eyes, the chart, and the next pair of gloves. Skin that looks dry can still carry organisms.

distractorExplanations.a: Rubbing the eyelids with unwashed hands moves organisms from glove removal onto the mucous membranes of the eye.
distractorExplanations.b: Dipping unwashed fingers into a shared lotion jar seeds the jar, so the next person picks up glove contamination with the lotion.
distractorExplanations.c: Putting the next pair on because the hands look dry skips hand hygiene and seals leftover organisms inside the new gloves.

prompt: Which item is considered a critical instrument (Spaulding) requiring sterilization?

options.text: Instruments that penetrate soft tissue or bone
Mouth mirrors that touch mucous membranes
Amalgam condensers that contact oral tissue
Radiograph positioning devices placed in the mouth

explanation: Critical items contact sterile tissue/vasculature and require sterilization. Examples include surgical instruments and periodontal scalers.

distractorExplanations.b: Mouth mirrors contact mucosa without penetrating tissue, which makes them semicritical items under the Spaulding classification.
distractorExplanations.c: CDC lists amalgam condensers as semicritical: they touch mucous membranes but do not penetrate soft tissue or bone.
distractorExplanations.d: Intraoral film/sensor holders contact mucous membranes only, so they are semicritical (heat-sterilize or high-level disinfect).

prompt: Semicritical instruments (contact mucous membranes) should be

options.text: Cleaned and wiped with an intermediate-level surface disinfectant between patients
Heat-sterilized when heat-tolerant; if heat-sensitive, use high-level disinfection
Sterilized only when they penetrate tissue; otherwise low-level disinfection suffices
Soaked in a high-level disinfectant as the first choice even when heat-tolerant

explanation: Semicritical items need sterilization or HLD depending on material tolerance. Follow the manufacturer's IFU for heat-sensitive items.

distractorExplanations.a: Intermediate-level disinfectants are for clinical contact surfaces and noncritical items; semicritical items need sterilization or HLD.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses semicritical with noncritical: low-level disinfection is for intact-skin items, while mucosal-contact items need sterilization or HLD.
distractorExplanations.d: CDC prefers heat sterilization for heat-tolerant semicritical items; chemical HLD is reserved for items that cannot withstand heat.

prompt: When should gloves be changed during patient care in dentistry?

options.text: After each patient by washing gloved hands, changing them only when torn
At the start and end of each session, unless a tear becomes visible
Between patients and whenever torn/contaminated during a procedure
Between patients, but a tear mid-procedure can wait until the appointment ends

explanation: Gloves are single-use barriers; change between patients and when integrity is compromised.

distractorExplanations.a: Washing gloves degrades the material and causes wicking; exam gloves are single-use and must be replaced between patients.
distractorExplanations.b: Session-based glove use carries contamination from one patient to the next; gloves are changed for every patient.
distractorExplanations.d: A torn glove is no longer a barrier, so it must be replaced promptly during the procedure, not at the end of the appointment.

prompt: Hand hygiene is required

options.text: After removing gloves, but not before donning a new pair
Before donning gloves; glove removal itself leaves hands clean
At the start of each session and whenever hands look soiled
Before donning gloves and after removing gloves

explanation: Hand hygiene is the core of standard precautions and is needed around glove use. Hand hygiene is also required whenever hands are visibly soiled.

distractorExplanations.a: Skips hand hygiene before gloving; contaminated hands transfer microbes onto the outside of new gloves as they are put on.
distractorExplanations.b: Hands are contaminated during glove removal and through glove micro-tears, so hand hygiene is required after removal too.
distractorExplanations.c: Session-start hygiene skips the per-patient moments around glove use; invisible contamination still requires hand hygiene.

prompt: A surgical mask in dentistry is primarily intended to:

options.text: Protect mucous membranes of the wearer from splash/spatter
Protect the wearer from airborne TB droplet nuclei in place of an N95 respirator
Protect the patient from the wearer's droplets, with no role in staff protection
Serve as eye and face protection without the need for separate eyewear

explanation: Masks are PPE for splash/droplet; they are not sterilizers and are not week-long single items. It also reduces the wearer's droplet exposure.

distractorExplanations.b: A surgical mask is not a respirator; airborne TB exposure calls for a fit-tested N95 or higher, not a surgical mask.
distractorExplanations.c: Under OSHA the mask is PPE for the wearer's nose and mouth against spatter; source control for the patient is a secondary benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: A mask covers only the nose and mouth; eyes still need goggles or a face shield when spatter is anticipated.

prompt: Eye protection should be worn

options.text: During surgical procedures, but not during routine hygiene or restorative care
When splash or spatter of blood/saliva is reasonably anticipated
By the operator only, since the assistant sits outside the spatter zone
When the patient has a known infectious disease noted in the medical history

explanation: Standard precautions call for eye protection with anticipated splash/spatter.

distractorExplanations.a: Ultrasonic scaling, handpieces, and air-water syringes create spatter during routine care, so eye protection is not limited to surgery.
distractorExplanations.c: The assistant is within the spatter range of the oral cavity and needs eye protection just like the operator.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard Precautions do not depend on disclosed disease; eye protection is driven by anticipated splash, not by the health history.

prompt: During scaling, the assistant feels a split in the exam glove while the scaler is still on the tooth. The assistant should

options.text: Cover the split with tape and finish the area before a glove change
Wipe the torn spot with alcohol and continue if the skin looks intact
Stop, remove the gloves, clean the hands, and don a new pair before going on
Finish the stroke, change gloves, and skip hand cleaning to save time

explanation: A split exam glove is no longer a barrier, so saliva can reach the skin and the skin can seed the mouth. The gloves come off, the hands are cleaned, and a new pair goes on before the scaler returns to the tooth. Tape, alcohol on the glove, or a delayed change leaves the break in the field.

distractorExplanations.a: Tape does not restore a glove barrier and traps moisture in the split, so the torn glove has to come off rather than be patched.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol on a torn glove weakens the material and leaves the hole open. The glove comes off and the hands are cleaned before a new pair.
distractorExplanations.d: Finishing the stroke keeps the open glove in saliva, and skipping hand hygiene places those organisms inside the new gloves.

prompt: During a sealant check the child coughs, and visible saliva speckles the clinician's mask. This exposure is best classed as

options.text: Droplet spread, with large saliva drops that fall and land nearby
Airborne spread by nuclei that stay aloft and need a fit-tested respirator
Percutaneous contact, the same path as a stick from a used needle
Indirect contact from a clipboard the previous patient handled

explanation: A cough throws large saliva droplets that fall onto a mask, the skin, and nearby surfaces. Visible speckles are that droplet spray, not a cloud of nuclei hanging in the room. A fit-tested respirator is for airborne precautions, not for drops that have already landed.

distractorExplanations.b: Airborne nuclei stay suspended and are the reason for a fit-tested respirator. Visible saliva on a mask has already landed, which is droplet spray.
distractorExplanations.c: Percutaneous spread needs a puncture through skin. Saliva that flew onto the mask did not pass through the skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Indirect contact moves organisms on an object from one person to another. This saliva left the child's mouth in the cough.

prompt: Before the first patient of the morning, the history form is blank and the patient reports feeling well. The assistant should

options.text: Finish the history for allergies and conditions, and still use Standard Precautions
Skip the history, because those precautions already cover every patient the same way
Add extra barriers if the finished form later names a bloodborne infection
Treat saliva as ordinary fluid unless the form mentions bleeding or hepatitis

explanation: The history is still completed because allergies, medicines, and conditions change how the visit is run. A blank form or a report of feeling well does not make saliva or blood safe. Standard Precautions treat that material as infectious for every patient.

distractorExplanations.b: Skipping the history misses a latex allergy, a bleeding risk, and other care changes. Standard Precautions do not replace that review.
distractorExplanations.c: Extra barriers triggered by a named bloodborne infection are the habit Universal Precautions replaced. Splash protection follows the procedure for every patient.
distractorExplanations.d: In dentistry saliva is treated as potentially infectious for every patient, whether or not the form mentions blood or hepatitis.

prompt: The clinician's hands are visibly dusty with pumice after polishing. Before pulling on the next pair of gloves, the clinician should

options.text: Wash with soap and water, because pumice leaves the hands visibly soiled
Use an alcohol rub, the product to pick whenever gloves have just come off
Skip both products because pumice is not blood and the gloves stayed intact
Rinse with water alone and save soap for the end of the clinical day

explanation: Visible soil, including pumice, polish, or blood, is washed off with soap and water. An alcohol-based rub is for hands that are not visibly soiled. Gloves do not cancel that step, and a water rinse leaves the grit and the organisms on the skin.

distractorExplanations.b: An alcohol rub is for hands that are not visibly soiled. Pumice and other visible soil need soap and water.
distractorExplanations.c: Soil does not have to be blood to need soap and water, and wearing gloves does not replace hand hygiene before the next pair.
distractorExplanations.d: A water rinse leaves pumice and organisms on the skin. Soap and water are the response to visible soil, not a once-a-day step.

prompt: Fresh nail extensions and chipped polish cover the assistant's fingertips at the start of a restorative visit. The right adjustment is to

options.text: Remove the extensions and chipped polish so the nails are short and clean
Leave the extensions and count on gloves to cover whatever sits underneath
Rub alcohol over the nail surfaces to clear debris under the tips
Keep the fresh extensions and remove only the chipped polish

explanation: Extensions and chipped polish hold debris that hand hygiene does not reach, and the edges puncture gloves. Nails for patient care should be short, smooth, and free of extensions and chipped polish before the gloves go on. A longer cuff does not clean what is under the nail.

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves do not reach debris under an extension, and long nails tear the glove. The extensions come off before patient care.
distractorExplanations.c: An alcohol rub does not clean the underside of an artificial nail. The extensions and chipped polish have to come off.
distractorExplanations.d: Fresh extensions still hold debris and can puncture the glove. Removing only the chipped polish leaves that risk in place.

prompt: Choosing gloves for a bloody extraction still leaves the face uncovered. Spray from the surgical handpiece is expected. For the assistant's face, the setup should include

options.text: A surgical mask, with eyewear left off because the operator stands closer
A mask and eye protection, because the assistant shares that spray zone
A fit-tested respirator used in place of both the mask and the eyewear
No face barrier, because the history names no infectious disease

explanation: Blood and saliva spray calls for a mask and eye protection on everyone in the zone, including the assistant. A respirator does not cover the eyes and is not the setup for ordinary splash. A quiet medical history does not cancel the barrier.

distractorExplanations.a: The assistant is in the same spray as the operator, so eye protection is part of the setup for both people.
distractorExplanations.c: A fit-tested respirator is for airborne precautions. It does not cover the eyes, and ordinary splash still needs eye protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard Precautions do not wait for a named infection. Anticipated blood and saliva spray is enough to require a mask and eye protection.

prompt: Sequence for putting on clinical attire before a surgical extraction is laid out on the counter. The gloves should go on

options.text: First, so the hands stay covered while the mask and eyewear are adjusted
Last, after the mask and eyewear, with cuffs pulled over the gown sleeves
Before the gown, so the sleeves can be pulled down over the gloves
After the patient is seated and the handpiece has already started to spray

explanation: Gloves go on last, after the gown, mask, and eyewear, so the cuffs cover the gown sleeves. Putting them on earlier soils them while the mask and eyewear are adjusted. Waiting until the handpiece is already spraying leaves the hands bare during the exposure.

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves put on first become soiled when the clinician adjusts the mask and eyewear. Face protection goes on before the gloves.
distractorExplanations.c: Gown sleeves belong under the glove cuffs. Pulling the gown down over the gloves leaves the wrists uncovered and soils the gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves go on before the handpiece starts, even if the patient is already seated. Starting the handpiece first exposes bare skin to spray.

prompt: Order for taking off soiled clinical wear is unsettled after the extraction. The gloves should come off

options.text: After the mask is pulled off by its front, gloves still on the hands
Before the mask and eyewear, so the face is handled after that pair is off
Last, after the eyelids have already been rubbed to clear fogging
After a soap wash performed while they are still worn on the hands

explanation: Gloves carry the most blood and saliva, so they come off before the mask or eyewear is handled. Face protection is then taken by the straps, not the front. Hand hygiene follows so organisms from the gloves are not carried to the eyes or the next patient.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling the mask off by the front with gloves still on plants the most soiled surface against the face. Gloves come off before the face is handled.
distractorExplanations.c: Rubbing the eyes while the gloves are still on transfers blood and saliva to the mucous membranes. The gloves come off before any face contact.
distractorExplanations.d: Washing exam gloves while they are worn damages them and wicks fluid through the material. They come off, and hand hygiene is done on the skin.

prompt: A damp mask from the morning patient is still tied in place as the next person sits. The assistant should

options.text: Keep wearing it through the whole afternoon if the color still looks even
Hang it to dry and tie the same mask on for the next patient
Discard it and put on a dry mask before the next patient is treated
Turn it inside out so the damp side faces away from the nose

explanation: A wet mask lets organisms through and no longer works as a splash barrier. The outside is also soiled by spray, so the mask is changed between patients as well as when it is damp. Drying it, flipping it, or wearing it all afternoon leaves that soil on the face.

distractorExplanations.a: Color is a poor check. A mask is changed when it is wet and between patients, even when it still looks uniform.
distractorExplanations.b: Hanging a mask to dry and putting it back on returns the soiled outer surface to the face for the next patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Turning a mask inside out places the contaminated outer surface against the nose and mouth.

prompt: Exam gloves from the last patient are still on while the assistant opens the clean supply drawer. The assistant should

options.text: Leave them on so a covered hand is what touches the clean drawer
Rinse them at the sink and then pick up supplies from the drawer
Remove them, clean the hands, and don a fresh pair for the next patient
Pull a new glove over each used one and then reach into the drawer

explanation: Exam gloves are single-patient items. Touching a drawer with the used pair moves saliva onto supplies the next patient will meet. The gloves come off, the hands are cleaned, and a new pair is donned for the next person.

distractorExplanations.a: Used gloves carry the last patient's saliva onto every item they touch, including a drawer that other patients' supplies come from.
distractorExplanations.b: Rinsing exam gloves damages them and wicks fluid through the material. They are discarded, not washed and reused.
distractorExplanations.d: A new glove over a used one keeps the contaminated glove on the hand and still soils the wrist as it reaches into the drawer.

prompt: The patient removes the protective glasses because they fog during a crown prep with a spraying handpiece. The assistant should

options.text: Let the glasses stay off, since patient eyewear is for surgical extractions
Move the clinician's face shield onto the patient and keep working
Pause and have the patient put the glasses back on before the handpiece restarts
Rely on the patient bib, which covers the eyes along with the clothing

explanation: Patients need eye protection when spray, debris, or a dropped instrument could reach the eyes. Fogging is uncomfortable, but it is not a reason to leave the eyes uncovered during a spraying prep. A bib covers clothing, and the clinician's face shield is that person's own barrier.

distractorExplanations.a: A spraying handpiece throws debris during restorative care, not just during extractions. The patient's glasses go back on before the prep continues.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving the clinician's face shield onto the patient strips the clinician's eye protection and does not replace glasses that fit the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: A bib shields clothing and skin on the chest. It does not cover the eyes.

prompt: A high-speed handpiece is cutting a filling prep, and neither a dam nor suction is running. To shrink the spatter, the team should

options.text: Trust the surgical masks to clear the spatter out of the room air
Aim a fan toward the patient and keep cutting with no dam and no suction
Place a dental dam to isolate the tooth and run high-volume evacuation
Have the patient hold cotton rolls in place of a dam and evacuation

explanation: A dental dam walls saliva away from the tooth, and high-volume evacuation captures spray at the mouth. Together they cut the spatter a high-speed handpiece throws. A mask protects the wearer's face and does not clear the room, and a fan or cotton rolls do not replace those two controls.

distractorExplanations.a: A surgical mask blocks spray onto the nose and mouth. It does not clear spatter from the room or sterilize the air.
distractorExplanations.b: A fan can push the cloud around the room. It does not isolate the tooth or capture spray at the mouth.
distractorExplanations.d: Cotton rolls retract tissue. They do not isolate saliva the way a dental dam does, and they do not capture spray the way high-volume evacuation does.

prompt: High-volume suction sits unused while an ultrasonic scaler floods the mouth with water. The assistant should

options.text: Leave the suction off so the patient avoids the chill of the airflow
Park a saliva ejector in the cheek and treat it as equal spray control
Aim a small fan across the mouth and leave the high-volume tip parked
Bring the high-volume tip next to the scaler so spray is caught at the mouth

explanation: An ultrasonic scaler throws water, saliva, and blood away from the tip. High-volume evacuation catches that spray where it is made. A saliva ejector removes pooled fluid, a fan blows the cloud around, and comfort is not a reason to leave the evacuator off.

distractorExplanations.a: Chill is a comfort issue. Leaving high-volume suction off lets the scaler spray travel onto the team and the room.
distractorExplanations.b: A saliva ejector clears fluid pooled in the mouth. It does not capture scaler spray the way high-volume evacuation does.
distractorExplanations.c: A fan spreads the cloud through the room. The high-volume tip has to sit at the mouth to catch the spray.

prompt: Cotton rolls sit beside the tooth while a spraying handpiece prepares a crown, and high-volume suction is already running. To keep saliva out of that spray, the team should

options.text: Mask the patient so saliva cannot leave the mouth with the spray
Lower the water and keep the cotton rolls as the isolation method
Have the patient breathe through the nose so saliva stays out of the spray
Isolate the prepared tooth with a dental dam so saliva stays off the bur

explanation: Cotton rolls do not seal saliva away from the tooth, so the handpiece still throws oral fluid. A dental dam isolates the tooth and keeps that saliva out of the spray. Suction is already capturing what leaves the mouth; the missing control is the dam, not a mask on the patient or a change in breathing.

distractorExplanations.a: A mask on the patient does not separate saliva from the tooth being cut. Isolation with a dam is what keeps oral fluid off the bur.
distractorExplanations.b: Less water may shrink the mist, but cotton rolls still let saliva reach the bur. The dam is the isolation barrier.
distractorExplanations.c: Nasal breathing does not wall saliva off from the tooth. A dental dam is what keeps that fluid out of the spray.

prompt: The room still smells of toothpaste after the last visit, and the same mask is about to stay on. The right correction is to

options.text: Keep the mask, because the toothpaste smell shows the air has cleared
Store the mask and wear that same one again for the rest of the week
Park the mask under the chin between patients and lift it back for treatment
Discard the mask, clean the hands, and don a new mask for the next patient

explanation: A mask is changed between patients because the outside is contaminated by spray, and it is changed again if it gets wet. Odor in the room is not a cleanliness test, and a mask does not sterilize the air. Hand hygiene goes with the change so the new mask is tied on with clean hands.

distractorExplanations.a: Room odor says nothing about contamination. A mask does not clear or sterilize the air, and it is changed between patients.
distractorExplanations.b: Saving a used mask for the rest of the week puts a soiled barrier back on the face for later patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Parking a mask under the chin soils the inside and the neck, then returns that soil to the nose and mouth.

prompt: A colleague reaches for a respirator before a routine prophy on a well patient and plans to skip eyewear. The assistant should point out that

options.text: A respirator also shields the eyes, so eyewear can come off for this prophy
Fit testing can wait when a respirator is used for a short routine prophy
Routine prophy spray is airborne spread, so the respirator is the full setup
A fit-tested respirator is for airborne precautions; splash still needs eyewear

explanation: An N95 or similar respirator is for airborne precautions after the wearer has been fit tested. A routine prophy produces splash and spatter, which a surgical mask and eye protection are meant to block. The respirator does not cover the eyes, so skipping eyewear leaves that route open.

distractorExplanations.a: A respirator covers the nose and mouth. It does not shield the eyes, so eyewear stays on when spray is expected.
distractorExplanations.b: Fit testing is what shows a respirator actually seals. A short visit does not waive it, and a routine prophy is not an airborne-precaution procedure.
distractorExplanations.c: Prophy spray is splash and droplet spatter, not an airborne-precaution event. A respirator is not the ordinary setup and does not replace eyewear.
